claims.text: Increasing the average valence electron count in a Ti-rich heavy-metal high-entropy alloy modifies its electron-phonon coupling strength.
Increasing the average valence electron count modifies the electronic density of states near the Fermi level.
Changes in electron-phonon coupling and Fermi-level density of states alter the superconducting transition temperature.
An equimolar Ti-Zr-Hf-Mo-W alloy satisfies the requirement that all five elements exceed 5 at.%.
The proposed equimolar Ti-Zr-Hf-Mo-W starting alloy forms a uniform disordered BCC solid solution.
Small substitutional composition changes can incrementally vary the alloy's average valence electron count.
XRD, TEM, and EDS can be used to verify phase homogeneity and the absence of secondary phases.
Arc melting followed by annealing at 1200°C for 24 hours in an inert atmosphere will promote a single-phase solid solution in the proposed alloy series.
The composition-adjusted alloys will retain a uniform disordered BCC structure with well-defined lattice parameters.
The lattice parameters will reflect an adjusted average electron density caused by the composition changes.
Maintaining phase purity ensures that observed superconducting changes are intrinsic to electron-count variation.
BCS theory provides the mechanism connecting valence-electron-dependent electronic and phononic properties to shifts in Tc.
Increased average valence electron count will produce a systematic shift, either enhancement or suppression, in Tc relative to the equimolar baseline.
Tc shifts will be accompanied by correlated changes in superconducting coherence length.
The equimolar Ti-rich baseline has an optimal electron concentration for intrinsic superconductivity in a BCC matrix.
The proposed relationship is applicable only while the alloys remain single-phase solid solutions and avoid FCC transformation or secondary precipitation.
Competing changes in electron-phonon coupling and density of states may produce a non-monotonic relationship between valence electron count and Tc.
An invariant or erratic Tc across phase-pure compositions with incrementally varied valence electron count would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as having an optimal electron concentration, which would normally imply that moving away from it suppresses Tc, while the prediction allows either enhancement or suppression without explaining how enhancement is compatible with baseline optimality.

The prediction requires a clear systematic trend, but the uncertainty permits non-monotonic behavior, while the falsification rule treats erratic behavior as falsifying. The hypothesis does not define how an acceptable non-monotonic trend is distinguished from falsifying erratic behavior.
